Neither. The premise is the problem: more agents don't always give better results.

Each agent you add has to be given context, makes its own model calls, and passes results back to the others. Your budget is small, so that cost matters. The reported numbers are rough: an agent uses about 4x the tokens of a plain chat, and a multi-agent system about 15x. Anthropic's own research system reportedly did much better than a single agent, but token usage explained most of that gain, so a lot of it was simply spending more. Their approach fits broad, parallel research tasks worth the extra spend. I only saw these figures in secondary write-ups, not Anthropic's original post, so check it before you quote them at your review.

A concrete example from your assistant. A student asks: "Can I use the laser cutter Thursday at 3?" That is one chain of steps: look up the training requirements in the manual, check the calendar, book. Each step needs the result of the one before. Splitting those across five or ten agents just adds handoffs where context can get lost, and you pay for every handoff.

Splitting can pay off when subtasks are independent and can run in parallel, or when one agent's context would get too large to handle. Your assistant doesn't look like that yet.

My recommendation for the design review is to start with one agent that has three tools: manual search, calendar check and booking. Make any fixed steps a plain workflow. Add a second agent only when you can name a specific failure that the split would fix.

Quick check: for the Thursday request, which of the three steps could run in parallel, and which couldn't?

I can also teach a short lesson on workflows versus agents and when multi-agent pays off.

Sources:
- [Secondary summary of Anthropic's multi-agent research system](https://www.implicator.ai/inside-claudes-research-engine-are-teams-of-ai-agents-the-future-of-artificial-intelligence/)
